metadata.file_name: 11. Demir & Karaboğa. (2021). Modeling mathematics achievement with deep learning methods.pdf
metadata.title: Modeling mathematics achievement with deep learning methods
metadata.venue: Sigma Journal of Engineering and Natural Sciences

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA 2018 Turkey survey data and constructs an analytic dataset by selecting the most successful 30% and the most unsuccessful 30% of students for mathematics achievement classification. The manuscript does not report whether PISA complex survey weights (student/sampling weights) or replicate weights were applied in model training or evaluation, so weight usage cannot be confirmed. Because the models are deep learning neural networks (Elman/Jordan) and other classifiers (MLP, logistic regression), the authors do not describe any weight-aware estimation procedure; this suggests weights may have been omitted, but this is not explicitly stated. The paper also does not document additional preprocessing such as missing-data handling, feature scaling, or outlier removal, beyond the success/failure subsampling.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The dependent variable is PV1MATH (Mathematical Achievement), indicating that a single plausible value draw was used as the target for classification. However, the manuscript does not report how missing questionnaire/test inputs were handled when building the feature set, which is a reporting gap because PISA datasets typically contain item nonresponse. Without documentation of missing-data treatment, model performance and generalizability may be sensitive to the implicit exclusion or imputation strategy used.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used PISA 2018 Turkey data and selected the most successful 30% and the most unsuccessful 30% of students to form a two-class dataset for mathematics achievement (success vs. unsuccessful). The target variable is PV1MATH, and the feature set includes the listed student background and ICT-related variables from Table 1.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2018 Turkey (Mathematics) — PV1MATH success vs. unsuccessful classification
main_findings.performance_metrics: Best model (Jordan neural network) — Test accuracy: 0.826; Test AUC: 0.739. Other test metrics: Elman NN accuracy 0.711 (AUC not reported), MLP accuracy 0.705 (AUC not reported), Logistic regression accuracy 0.671 (AUC not reported). Reported additional test metrics for Jordan: Sensitivity 0.826, Specificity 0.869, False Positive Rate 0.131, F1-score 0.826.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 Turkey the study leveraged Gender, Sense of belonging, ESCS socioeconomic index, Home possessions, and Parents’ emotional support (plus ICT-related variables) to classify students into successful vs. unsuccessful mathematics achievement using PV1MATH, finding that the Jordan neural network achieved the highest test accuracy (0.826) and AUC (0.739) among compared models. This indicates that deep learning models can improve the prediction of mathematics achievement status from student background and ICT context, suggesting that education authorities could use such models to target support for students with low belonging, weaker socioeconomic resources, and limited home/digital learning access, while noting that the paper does not document survey-weight use or missing-data handling.

data.outcome_summary: The study uses PISA 2018 Turkey mathematics data and builds a binary classification task for mathematics achievement using PV1MATH, selecting the most successful 30% and most unsuccessful 30% of students. It compares deep learning models (Elman neural network and Jordan neural network) against a multilayer perceptron and logistic regression. On the test set, the Jordan neural network performs best with accuracy 0.826 and AUC 0.739, with sensitivity 0.826, specificity 0.869, and F1-score 0.826. The paper reports that gender, sense of belonging, ESCS, home possessions, parents’ emotional support, ICT available at home, and digital device use in lessons are effective for predicting success. Limitations include lack of reported survey-weight application and missing-data handling, and the use of PV1MATH as a single plausible value for the target.
